questions.text: Why observe the browser again after executing a GUI action?

options.A: To assume the requested state change succeeded without checking it.
options.B: To replace every future action with the original fixed plan.
options.C: To avoid passing action outcomes back into the planning loop.
options.D: To check the resulting state and adjust the next action if needed.

questions.explanation: An observation closes the feedback loop: actions can fail or produce unexpected state, so the next decision should use the updated evidence.

questions.text: A button moved after a page update, so an old click coordinate is stale. What is the best next step?

options.A: Repeat the same coordinate until the step budget expires.
options.B: Use the current screenshot or accessibility tree to locate the target again.
options.C: Mark the task complete because the earlier plan named the right button.
options.D: Drop all observations and continue the remaining actions unchanged.

questions.explanation: Grounding must use the current UI state. A semantic target description plus fresh screenshot or accessibility evidence allows the target to be located again.

questions.text: run_task applies every planned action and then checks state.page==expected_page. apply_action treats done as a no-op. If page is confirmation, expected_page is reset_sent, and done says success=True, what is the reported success?

options.A: False, because the final page does not match expected_page.
options.B: True, because the done action explicitly claims success.
options.C: True, because any terminal action changes the page to expected_page.
options.D: An exception, because a done action must overwrite the page.

questions.explanation: Success comes from the final state comparison, not the supplied done.success flag. A done action leaves page unchanged, so confirmation != reset_sent yieldsFalse.
